triage.reason: Pediatric genital exam finding reachable by history and physical exam, with clear workup and management decisions including timing of orchiopexy.

demographics: Occurs in about 1–4% of full-term newborn boys and up to 30% of preterm boys
More common in premature and low-birth-weight infants
Often detected at birth or during well-child visits in the first year

risk_factors.text: Low birth weight or small for gestational age
Maternal smoking or alcohol use during pregnancy

family_history: Undescended testis in a father or brother

chief_complaints.text: The doctor says one of his testicles hasn't come down
I can't feel one of his testicles in the sac
There's a little bulge in his groin

hpi.onset: Present from birth; noticed at the newborn exam or during a well-child visit
hpi.duration: Since birth; may persist beyond 6 months of age
hpi.progression: The testis may descend on its own in the first few months of life, especially in preterm infants; if it remains undescended after 6 months, spontaneous descent is unlikely
hpi.location: One or both sides; the testis may be in the inguinal canal, abdomen, or ectopic position
hpi.quality: Painless; the scrotum on the affected side may look smaller or less full
hpi.severity: Not painful; mainly a concern about future fertility and cancer risk

associated_symptoms.text: Small scrotum on the affected side

pertinent_negatives: Pain or tenderness in the groin or scrotum
Swelling or redness of the scrotum
Vomiting or abdominal distention suggesting bowel obstruction

positives.text: One testis not palpable in the scrotum
Small scrotum on the affected side
Groin bulge that comes and goes

atypical.how_it_differs: Older boys may present with an empty scrotum noticed late, or with a retractile testis that ascends intermittently; a truly undescended testis remains out of the scrotum.
Preterm infants have a higher rate of undescended testes, and descent may still occur in the first months after birth.

general.mild: Well-appearing, thriving infant or young boy; no distress
general.moderate: Well-appearing but with an associated inguinal hernia or a testis that intermittently retracts
general.severe: Ill-appearing with a tender, irreducible groin mass suggesting incarceration
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic, with a firm tender groin mass and signs of bowel obstruction

findings.maneuver: Palpate the scrotum on the affected side between thumb and fingers
findings.finding: The testis is not palpable in the scrotum

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the scrotum, comparing both sides
findings.finding: The affected hemiscrotum is smaller and less full than the other side

findings.maneuver: Palpate along the inguinal canal from the internal ring toward the scrotum
findings.finding: A firm, mobile, oval mass consistent with an undescended testis in the inguinal canal

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal canal and abdomen after the scrotal exam
findings.finding: No testis can be felt anywhere along the expected path of descent

findings.maneuver: Gently milk the testis down from the inguinal canal into the scrotum and then release
findings.finding: The testis can be brought into the scrotum and stays there briefly before retracting back up

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the groin for a bulge, and ask the parent if it comes and goes
findings.finding: A soft, reducible groin bulge consistent with an inguinal hernia

findings.maneuver: Inspect the position of the urethral meatus on the ventral penis
findings.finding: The urethral meatus opens on the ventral surface of the penis rather than at the tip

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scrotal skin for redness, induration or discoloration
findings.finding: Scrotal skin is normal in color and texture

findings.maneuver: Palpate the palpable testis and the scrotal contents gently
findings.finding: No tenderness on palpation of the descended testis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for masses, distention or tenderness
findings.finding: Abdomen is soft, non-distended and non-tender

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure
findings.finding: Vital signs are within normal limits for age

findings.text: Testis identified in the inguinal canal
No testis identified along the expected path of descent (suggests intra-abdominal or absent testis)
Smaller testis on the affected side compared with the contralateral testis

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Ultrasound is nondiagnostic and the testis remains nonpalpable

findings.text: Testis localized in the abdomen or inguinal canal
No testis identified (suggests testicular agenesis or atrophy)
Testis visualized in the abdomen or inguinal canal
Blind-ending spermatic vessels consistent with testicular agenesis
Vessels entering the internal inguinal ring, suggesting an intracanalicular testis

initial.why: Localizes a nonpalpable testis and evaluates for associated inguinal hernia

confirmatory.why: Definitive localization and diagnosis when the testis is nonpalpable and imaging is nondiagnostic

supporting.test: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
supporting.why: May localize a nonpalpable testis when ultrasound is nondiagnostic
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is nondiagnostic and the testis remains nonpalpable

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of an undescended testis
No role in the evaluation of an undescended testis
No role in the evaluation of an undescended testis
Not used to evaluate an undescended testis in a male child
Not needed when the testis is palpable in the inguinal canal or scrotum

decision_points: A palpable testis in the inguinal canal or scrotum does not require imaging before referral
Nonpalpable testis warrants ultrasound and, if nondiagnostic, diagnostic laparoscopy
Orchiopexy is recommended by 6 to 18 months of age to preserve fertility and allow surveillance

differential.name: Retractile testis
differential.why_considered: An empty or apparently empty hemiscrotum in a young boy is most often a retractile testis, which is a normal variant rather than true cryptorchidism.

history: The testis is seen in the scrotum at times, especially in a warm bath or when relaxed
Parents report the testis comes and goes
No history of prematurity or family history of undescended testis
exam: The testis can be milked down into the scrotum and stays there briefly before retracting
The testis reaches the bottom of the scrotum with gentle traction
No inguinal mass is felt after the testis is brought down
imaging: Ultrasound is not needed; if done, the testis is normally positioned and sized

differential.name: Testicular agenesis (vanishing testis)
differential.why_considered: A truly nonpalpable testis may be absent rather than undescended, and this changes counseling and surgery.

history: The testis has never been felt on the affected side
No groin bulge or history of a palpable testis
exam: No testis palpable in the scrotum, inguinal canal or abdomen
Small or flat hemiscrotum on the affected side
labs: Karyotype and hormone testing only if a disorder of sex development is suspected
imaging: Ultrasound and MRI do not identify a testis

differential.name: Inguinal hernia
differential.why_considered: An inguinal bulge in an infant or young boy can be mistaken for an undescended testis, and the two often coexist.
differential.trigger: A groin bulge that is tender, irreducible, or accompanied by vomiting and abdominal distention

history: A groin bulge that comes and goes, worse with crying or straining
Vomiting or abdominal distention if incarcerated
exam: A soft, reducible bulge above the inguinal ring
The testis may be palpable separately in the scrotum
labs: No specific labs; CBC and electrolytes if incarceration or bowel obstruction is suspected
imaging: Ultrasound of the groin may show bowel or omentum in the canal
Abdominal radiograph or ultrasound if obstruction is suspected

differential.name: Disorder of sex development
differential.why_considered: A nonpalpable testis with ambiguous genitalia or hypospadias may reflect a disorder of sex development rather than isolated cryptorchidism.
differential.trigger: Ambiguous genitalia, severe hypospadias, or bilateral nonpalpable testes

history: Family history of ambiguous genitalia or unexplained neonatal death
Salt-wasting crisis in the newborn period
exam: Hyperpigmentation or signs of adrenal insufficiency
labs: Serum electrolytes and glucose if adrenal crisis is suspected
17-hydroxyprogesterone and other hormone testing as directed by pediatric endocrinology
imaging: Pelvic ultrasound to look for Müllerian structures
Genitography or MRI as directed by the specialist team

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: Acute scrotal pain and swelling can be confused with an undescended testis that has torsed, and torsion is a surgical emergency.
differential.trigger: Acute severe scrotal or groin pain with nausea and vomiting

history: No prior history of an empty scrotum
exam: Tender, high-riding testis with an abnormal lie
labs: No specific labs; urinalysis to exclude infection
imaging: Doppler ultrasound showing reduced or absent blood flow to the testis

differential.name: Testicular tumor
differential.why_considered: A painless testicular or groin mass in an older boy or young man may be a germ cell tumor, and cryptorchidism is a risk factor.
differential.trigger: A firm, painless testicular or groin mass, especially in an adolescent or young adult

history: Painless enlargement or heaviness of the testis
History of an undescended testis, even if corrected
exam: A firm, non-tender mass in the testis or inguinal canal
The mass does not reduce or transilluminate
labs: Alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG and LDH if a germ cell tumor is suspected
imaging: Scrotal ultrasound showing a solid intratesticular mass
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging if malignancy is confirmed

severity.mild: Unilateral undescended testis in an otherwise healthy full-term infant, palpable in the inguinal canal, with a normal scrotum on the other side and no associated hernia.
severity.moderate: Bilateral undescended testes or a unilateral undescended testis with an associated reducible inguinal hernia, or a testis that remains undescended after 6 months of age.
severity.severe: Nonpalpable testis, or an undescended testis with an incarcerated inguinal hernia causing a tender, irreducible groin mass and possible bowel obstruction.
severity.critical: Not applicable; cryptorchidism itself is not life-threatening, but an incarcerated or strangulated hernia with bowel ischemia or sepsis is a surgical emergency.

red_flags.finding: Tender, irreducible groin mass with vomiting or abdominal distention
red_flags.meaning: Incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia; needs urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Acute severe scrotal or groin pain with nausea and vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Testicular torsion until proven otherwise; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Ambiguous genitalia or bilateral nonpalpable testes
red_flags.meaning: Possible disorder of sex development; requires urgent endocrine and genetic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Firm, painless testicular or groin mass in an adolescent or young man
red_flags.meaning: Possible testicular germ cell tumor; requires urgent urologic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Signs of adrenal insufficiency such as hypotension, hyponatremia or hyperkalemia in a newborn with ambiguous genitalia
red_flags.meaning: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with salt-wasting crisis; life-threatening if untreated

complications.name: Testicular germ cell tumor
clues: History of an undescended testis, even after orchiopexy

complications.name: Testicular torsion of the undescended testis
clues: Acute severe groin or abdominal pain
Tender mass along the path of descent

complications.name: Psychological distress related to body image and fertility concerns
clues: Adolescent or young adult with anxiety about fertility or appearance

special_populations.differences: Preterm and low-birth-weight infants have a higher rate of undescended testes, and spontaneous descent may still occur in the first few months after birth; orchiopexy is generally recommended by 6 to 18 months of age if the testis remains undescended.
Older boys may present with a late-noticed empty scrotum or a retractile testis that ascends intermittently; a truly undescended testis remains out of the scrotum and requires referral.
Cryptorchidism is usually corrected in childhood; an adult with a history of an undescended testis remains at increased risk of testicular cancer and should be counseled on self-examination.

key_questions.question: Was the testicle ever felt in the scrotum, or has it always been missing?
key_questions.looking_for: Never palpated in the scrotum suggests a true undescended testis; intermittently present suggests a retractile testis

key_questions.question: When was it first noticed, and has it ever come down on its own?
key_questions.looking_for: Present since birth; spontaneous descent after 6 months is unlikely

key_questions.question: Is it one side or both sides?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilateral involvement raises concern for a disorder of sex development

key_questions.question: Was he born early or small for his dates?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity or low birth weight, the strongest risk factors

key_questions.question: Does he have a groin bulge that comes and goes, or that he cries and strains with?
key_questions.looking_for: Associated inguinal hernia, which often coexists

key_questions.question: Has he had any vomiting, abdominal swelling, or a bulge that won't go back in?
key_questions.looking_for: Incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia requiring urgent surgery

key_questions.question: Has he had any sudden severe pain in the groin or scrotum with nausea or vomiting?
Does anyone in the family have an undescended testis or a problem with genital development?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of undescended testis or a disorder of sex development

key_questions.question: Did the pregnancy involve smoking, alcohol, diabetes, or obesity?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal exposures weakly associated with cryptorchidism

key_questions.question: Has he had any urinary symptoms such as burning, blood in the urine, or trouble urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a urinary tract problem rather than cryptorchidism

key_questions.question: Was the penis normal at birth, or was the urine opening not at the tip?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypospadias or ambiguous genitalia suggesting a disorder of sex development

key_questions.question: Has he had any prior groin or scrotal surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior orchiopexy or hernia repair that may explain the current exam

reasoning_points: A testis that has never been palpated in the scrotum and remains out of the scrotum on examination
The affected hemiscrotum is smaller and less full than the other side
A firm, mobile mass may be felt along the inguinal canal, or no testis may be palpable anywhere
A retractile testis can be milked down into the scrotum and stays there briefly, which argues against true cryptorchidism
Prematurity and low birth weight are the strongest risk factors
Associated inguinal hernia, hypospadias, or ambiguous genitalia should be sought
Bilateral nonpalpable testes or ambiguous genitalia raise concern for a disorder of sex development
Imaging and diagnostic laparoscopy are reserved for the nonpalpable testis
Orchiopexy is recommended by 6 to 18 months of age to preserve fertility and allow surveillance

easy: Full-term newborn boy with an empty hemiscrotum noted at the newborn exam
Testis palpable in the inguinal canal
Smaller scrotum on the affected side
No acute pain, vomiting, or systemic symptoms
medium: Preterm infant in whom spontaneous descent may still occur in the first months
Retractile testis that intermittently ascends and must be distinguished from a true undescended testis
hard: Nonpalpable testis requiring ultrasound and diagnostic laparoscopy
Testis that remains undescended after 6 months of age
Ambiguous genitalia or severe hypospadias suggesting a disorder of sex development
Older boy or adolescent with a late-noticed empty scrotum
Undescended testis with an incarcerated inguinal hernia causing a tender, irreducible groin mass
